title: Ephemeral Plugin Priority Playbook
author: Evan Chu
body:
Summary:
This playbook describes the recommended priority arbitration, telemetry, and operational patterns for ephemeral plugins and extension runtimes that run inside the serving runtime process or as proxied microservices. Ephemeral plugins (feature adapters, custom prerun hooks, third-party tokenizers) can introduce variable latency and resource pressure; this document defines guardrails to preserve SLOs, avoid priority inversion, and safely degrade plugin behavior under strain.

Context and motivation:
- Ephemeral plugins are lightweight processes or in-process extensions loaded per-request or per-session to modify prompts, validate outputs, or call external enrichment services.
- Because they are often developed independently (customer-provided or third-party), they are a frequent source of tail-latency and unpredictable kernel-choice interactions (e.g., plugins that increase sequence length causing kernel breakpoints).
- The goal is to allow extensibility while maintaining the serving runtime's latency SLOs and cost bounds.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood Inference runtime versions that support the extension-plugin API (v2+) and the priority arbitration shim.
- Covers both in-process ephemeral plugins and proxied plugin backends.
- Does not cover persistent background services nor compile-time kernel changes.

Ownership and contacts:
- Runtime scheduling and plugin safety: eng-serving-runtime (primary)
- Observability and alerts: eng-platform (secondary)
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre (see runbook section)

Key principles:
1) Demand-fence early: classify plugin calls as potentially latency-sensitive and treat them as early-stage resource candidates (before kernel selection).
2) Fail fast and degrade predictably: define conservative time budgets and safe fallbacks for all plugin categories.
3) Telemetry-driven policy: use rolling telemetry windows (p95/p99) to automatically adjust priority weights and enable graceful shedding.
4) Quantization- and kernel-aware: plugin-induced sequence or token changes must be signalled to the kernel mapper so the scheduler can choose kernels that avoid long-tail regressions.

Plugin classification and default budgets:
- Type A: Latency-critical (e.g., token filters used in the final decode loop) — default budget 20ms.
- Type B: Inline enrichment (e.g., prompt expansion, metadata injection) — default budget 75ms.
- Type C: Non-blocking analytics or telemetry enrichment — default budget 250ms (execute as background or sampled paths).

Configuration table (example, YAML-style fields shown as a table):
| field | description | default |
|---|---|---|
| plugin.class | One of [A, B, C] | B |
| plugin.max_latency_ms | Max allowed wall time per invocation | 75 |
| plugin.priority_weight | Relative weight for scheduler | 100 |
| plugin.cpu_isolate | Whether plugin requires vCPU isolation | false |
| plugin.kv_cache_hint | Hint if plugin extends sequence length | none |
| plugin.fallback_mode | "skip" | "skip" |

Example runtime policy snippet (textual example):
- policy:
  - match: request.extension == "token-augment" AND request.model.family == "redwood-*/gpt"
    action:
      plugin.class: B
      plugin.max_latency_ms: 50
      plugin.priority_weight: 80
      plugin.fallback_mode: skip

Telemetry signals to collect (mandatory):
- plugin.invocations.count (per-plugin)
- plugin.latency.p50/p95/p99 (per-plugin, rolling 1m/5m/1h)
- plugin.error.rate (HTTP 5xx, timeouts, exceptions)
- kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin (histogram)
- request.tail-latency.delta when plugin enabled vs disabled (sampled)

Policy automation rules (examples):
1) Auto-shed: If plugin.latency.p99 > 3 * plugin.max_latency_ms for 2 consecutive 5m windows AND plugin.error.rate > 2%, mark plugin as deferred for new requests and set fallback_mode to "skip".
2) Down-weight: If total system CPU utilization > 85% and plugin.p95 > 2x baseline, reduce plugin.priority_weight by 50% for 10 minutes.
3) Kernel hint propagation: If kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin histogram shows >5% of requests crossing a kernel break point, add a routing hint to use long-seq-optimized kernels for requests that match this plugin pattern.

Graceful degradation patterns:
- Skip mode: Plugin is not executed; log event and add telemetry tag plugin.skipped=true.
- Async mode: Return immediately and enqueue best-effort enrichment; annotate response with enrichment.pending=true.
- Throttle mode: Rate-limit plugin invocations per tenant to a configured RPS.

Runbook: Immediate mitigation steps for plugin-related latency incidents
1) Detect: Pager triggers when global request.p99 increases > 25% and plugin-tagged requests show disproportionate delta (plugin.delta.p99 > 30ms).
2) Triage: Query telemetry for plugin.latency.p99 (1m,5m,1h) and kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin histogram.
3) Short-lived mitigation (1–10 minutes):
   a) Toggle plugin.fallback_mode to skip for the offending plugin across the fleet (or per-region).
   b) Apply rate-limits to plugin invocations at the gateway: curl -X PATCH https://controlplane/api/plugins/{id}/policy -d '{"max_rps": 10}'
4) Stabilize (10–60 minutes):
   a) If sequence-length growth caused kernel breakpoints, route affected traffic to long-seq-optimized model variants or reserve dedicated kernel slots.
   b) If CPU pressure is root cause, reduce plugin.priority_weight globally by 50% and enable async mode for non-critical classes.
5) Postmortem: Add findings to incident report, update plugin onboarding checklist with discovered failure modes.

Canary and rollout guidance for new ephemeral plugins:
- Local dev: run the plugin in the sandboxed runtime with --sample-rate=1% and collect latency histograms for at least 1000 requests.
- Canary stage: Deploy to 2% of production traffic with full telemetry and automatic abort if plugin.latency.p99 > 2x baseline or error.rate > 1% for 10 minutes.
- Gradual ramp: 2% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100% with manual review at each step.

Example alerting thresholds (suggested):
- Severity: P1 (page oncall): plugin.latency.p99 (5m) > 3x configured max_latency_ms AND plugin.error.rate > 2%
- Severity: P2 (notify team): plugin.latency.p95 (5m) > 2x configured max_latency_ms
- Severity: P3: plugin.error.rate (1h) > 0.5%

Developer onboarding checklist for plugin authors:
1) Declare plugin.class and max_latency_ms in manifest.yaml.
2) Provide a compatibility shim for sequence-length hints when the plugin mutates token counts.
3) Add unit tests that simulate slow external backends and assert fallback behavior.
4) Include telemetry tags: plugin.name, plugin.version, plugin.owner.
5) Run local sandbox suite (>=1k synthetic requests) and upload profiling output to the runtime profiling dashboard.

Operational notes and caveats:
- Quantized kernels may amplify tail effects if plugins introduce additional tokens; always validate plugin behavior with the quantized model variants used in production.
- In-process plugins bypass some OS-level isolation; prefer proxied plugins for untrusted third-party code.
- Priority weights are relative; ensure tenant-level fairness rules are enforced downstream of weight changes to avoid starvation.

Appendix: Example plugin manifest (manifest.yaml)
---
name: redwood-token-augment
version: 0.6.2
owner: team-extensibility
plugin.class: B
max_latency_ms: 50
priority_weight: 80
kv_cache_hint: increases_by_up_to: 32
fallback_mode: skip
---

Appendix: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
- Is the plugin running in-process or proxied? Proxied reduces blast radius.
- Are kernel hints emitted? If not, enable sequence-length-post-plugin sampling.
- Does disabling the plugin reduce tail latency? If yes, follow runbook mitigation and schedule a full regression test.

Related work and references:
- See scheduler policy language and warmstart docs for how priority_weight is translated into kernel slot allocation.
- See runtime telemetry sampling guide for how to collect and store plugin histograms.

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft and internal trial with two customer plugins.
- 2026-02-10: Added automation rules and example manifests after canary evaluation.

Tags: plugin-safety, priority-arbitration, runtime-playbook
